title: SYSK’s Fall True Crime Playlist: The Strange Unsolved Murder of Ken McElroy
summary: A Stuff You Should Know true crime playlist episode on Ken Rex McElroy, a violent career criminal in Skidmore, Missouri, who evaded convictions through intimidation and was shot to death in 1981 outside the D&NG Tavern in front of a crowd of townspeople who would not identify the shooters. The hosts cover his cattle theft, the 1976 shooting of Romaine Henry, his sexual abuse of underage girls and serial marriages, the 1980 shooting of grocer Ernest Bowen Camp, his bond revocation attempt, the mob confrontation and killing, the failed investigation, Trina McElroy's civil suit, and the attorney and highway patrolman involved. Also covers a brief listener mail segment about the Kenton Grua Grand Canyon speed record episode. Includes a trigger warning for sexual assault of minors.
topics: No One Saw a Thing documentary

segments.title: Cold open teaser
segments.summary: Teaser introducing the Ken McElroy murder as a true crime story of small town justice, later adapted into a movie.

segments.title: Opening banter and episode setup
segments.summary: Hosts open the episode, note it is an early January-style pick-me-up relative to Jonestown, and introduce McElroy and prior media about him.

segments.title: Prior media: book, documentary, and 1991 TV movie
segments.summary: Discussion of the 1988 book In Broad Daylight by Harry MacLean, the documentary No One Saw a Thing, and the 1991 TV movie starring Brian Dennehy and Marcia Gay Harden.
topics: No One Saw a Thing documentary

segments.title: McElroy's early life and head injury
segments.summary: McElroy was born in 1934 as one of sixteen children in Skidmore, Missouri, and started criminal activity young. At eighteen he was hit in the head by falling cribbing at a construction site, which the hosts note may have contributed to later behavior.

segments.title: Cattle theft and money
segments.summary: McElroy made money from crime, including cattle theft, hunting dog training and antiques dealing. Skidmore's county led the state in cattle thefts the year before his death, largely attributed to him.

segments.title: Attorney Richard Gene McFadden
segments.summary: McElroy was charged at least twenty-one times without conviction, aided by attorney Richard Gene McFadden, who was paid in cash.

segments.title: Witness and juror intimidation
segments.summary: McFadden used procedural delays while McElroy intimidated witnesses and jurors with threats, driveway parking, gunfire and arson threats, so cases collapsed.

segments.title: 1976 shooting of Romaine Henry
segments.summary: McElroy shot Romaine Henry in the stomach with a shotgun in July 1976 after Henry asked him to stop shooting pheasants out of season on his land. Friends provided alibis and he was not convicted.

segments.title: Threats to lawmen and officials
segments.summary: Highway patrolman Richard Stratton had run-ins with McElroy; McElroy threatened his family and held a shotgun to Stratton's wife Margaret. The county magistrate moved cases to other counties out of fear.

segments.title: Ad break
segments.summary: Mid-episode sponsor break.

segments.title: Child sexual abuse, serial marriages, and Trina McElroy
segments.summary: The hosts describe McElroy's sexual abuse and rape of underage girls, his serial marriages to avoid their testimony, the marriage to Trina McLeod when she was about fifteen with attorney McFadden as witness, her return to him after foster placement, and the arson of her parents' house. Content warning applies.

segments.title: 1980 shooting of Ernest Bowen Camp and threats to clergy
segments.summary: In 1980 McElroy's young daughter was caught shoplifting from the Bowen Camp grocery; McElroy then shot Ernest Bowen Camp through the neck in July that year. The minister Tim Warren was threatened when trying to visit Lois Bowen Camp.

segments.title: Town marshal and prosecution of McElroy
segments.summary: Town marshal David Dunbar quit after McElroy held him at gunpoint. The sheriff was slow to respond. Prosecutor David Baird, newly appointed, won a second-degree assault conviction and a two-year sentence, but McFadden appealed and McElroy was released on forty thousand dollars bail.

segments.title: Threats at the D&NG Tavern and bond revocation
segments.summary: Out on bail, McElroy displayed an M1 carbine at the D&NG Tavern and said he would finish off Bowen Camp. Pete Ward and his sons filed complaints, and a bond hearing was set.

segments.title: Ad break
segments.summary: Sponsor break after the bond hearing setup.

segments.title: American Legion meeting, tavern confrontation, and shooting
segments.summary: Around a hundred adults gathered at the American Legion Hall. Sheriff Danny Estes suggested following McElroy. Sixty or so people confronted him at the D&NG Tavern, then followed him out. As McElroy sat in his Silverado with Trina, he was shot in the head and neck by people with high-powered rifles, and the truck crashed after his foot hit the gas.

segments.title: Aftermath and witness silence
segments.summary: The autopsy found two different calibers of bullets. Witnesses would not speak. Trina said she saw Del Clement shoot McElroy with a deer rifle. One witness said Clement and another man sped off, but recanted. Trina was hustled into a bank.

segments.title: Rumors, investigation, and the FBI closing the case
segments.summary: Unverified rumors that the gun was thrown in a river and the head was kept in a freezer, and comments from Britt Small. Trina's newspaper accounts show fear. The FBI closed its investigation September 2, 1982, with no charges. Police chief Hal Riddle called it his most frustrating case.

segments.title: Reflections on mob justice
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the failure of local institutions and whether vigilante justice was justified, concluding that the town was probably better off without McElroy even though mob justice is wrong.

segments.title: Aftermath for Clement, Trina, and attorney McFadden
segments.summary: Del Clement died in 2009 without comment. Trina sued for wrongful death in 1985 for five million, settled for seventeen thousand six hundred, remarried, and died in 2012. McFadden was a lobbyist and died in 2012. A five thousand dollar reward was offered against anticipated movie rights.

segments.title: Stratton's regret and remaining mysteries
segments.summary: Richard Stratton said in an interview that the town acted because the law failed, and that he knew who did it but would never say. The hosts note the second shooter remains unidentified.

segments.title: Episode wrap-up
segments.summary: Hosts sign off on the McElroy story and transition to listener mail.

segments.title: Listener mail: Kenton Grua follow-up
segments.summary: A listener named Noah followed up on the Kenton Grua Grand Canyon speed record episode, explaining the eleven pm start was tied to timing the rapids so the flip would happen midday.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Standard sign-off and production credit, with listener email address given.
